title: What Arduino is
text: Arduino is an open-source electronics platform combining simple microcontroller boards with a free development environment. It lets people read inputs such as a button press, a light level, or a sensor reading, and turn them into outputs such as switching on an LED, driving a motor, or publishing data to a network service.

title: Open-source hardware and software
text: Both the Arduino board designs and the Arduino development software are released under open licences. Schematics and board files are published, so anyone may study, modify, manufacture, or sell compatible hardware. This openness is why so many third-party boards, clones, and derivative designs exist alongside the official products.

title: Why beginners choose Arduino
text: Arduino hides most of the complexity of embedded development. There is no need to configure registers, set up a toolchain, or buy a hardware programmer. A beginner can plug in a USB cable, install one program, and have a blinking LED within minutes, which makes it a common entry point into electronics.

title: Microcontroller versus microprocessor
text: A microcontroller is a complete small computer on a single chip, containing a processor core, memory, and input-output peripherals. A microprocessor holds only the processing core and depends on external memory and support chips. Arduino boards are built around microcontrollers, which is why they boot instantly and run a single program forever.

title: Arduino compared with Raspberry Pi
text: A Raspberry Pi is a small Linux computer with an operating system, multitasking, and video output. An Arduino runs one program directly on bare metal with no operating system. Arduino excels at precise real-time control of electrical signals, while a Raspberry Pi suits tasks needing networking, storage, or a graphical display.

title: The Arduino IDE
text: The Arduino IDE is the desktop application used to write, compile, and upload programs. It provides a text editor, a board and port selector, a verify button that compiles code, an upload button that transfers it to the board, and a serial monitor for viewing text sent back from the board.

title: What a sketch is
text: An Arduino program is called a sketch. It is saved as a file with a .ino extension inside a folder of the same name. A sketch is compiled into machine code for the specific microcontroller on the selected board and then written into the board's flash memory, where it runs on every power-up.

title: The Arduino programming language
text: Arduino code is C++ with a simplified set of built-in functions and automatic handling of some boilerplate. Because it is really C++, standard control structures, arithmetic, functions, arrays, classes, and pointers all work. Most beginners never need the advanced features, but they are available when a project grows more demanding.

title: Compile and upload cycle
text: Pressing verify compiles the sketch into a binary and reports syntax errors without touching the board. Pressing upload compiles and then transfers the binary over USB into the microcontroller's flash. The board resets automatically and begins running the new program, replacing whatever sketch was stored previously.

title: The community and shared code
text: A very large community publishes tutorials, wiring diagrams, forum answers, and reusable libraries. For almost any common sensor or display there is already example code available. This shared body of work substantially reduces the effort required to get an unfamiliar component working for the first time.

title: Arduino Uno
text: The Arduino Uno is the most widely used board and the usual reference for tutorials. It carries an ATmega328P microcontroller, fourteen digital pins, six analog inputs, a USB socket, a barrel power jack, and a reset button. Its through-hole friendly layout and wide shield compatibility make it a dependable default choice.

title: Arduino Uno pin layout
text: The Uno exposes digital pins numbered zero to thirteen along one edge, with six of them capable of PWM output. The opposite edge carries analog inputs A0 to A5 plus power pins supplying 5V, 3.3V, ground, and VIN. Headers are spaced so that stackable shields align with them directly.

title: Arduino Nano
text: The Arduino Nano packs essentially the same capability as the Uno into a much smaller board with pins arranged for breadboard use. It suits finished projects and tight enclosures where the Uno is physically too large. It lacks a barrel jack, so power arrives over USB or through its VIN pin.

title: Arduino Mega 2560
text: The Mega 2560 targets projects that outgrow the Uno's pin count. It offers fifty-four digital pins, sixteen analog inputs, four hardware serial ports, and considerably more flash and SRAM. It is commonly chosen for large LED installations, complex robots, and 3D printer control boards.

title: Arduino Leonardo
text: The Leonardo uses an ATmega32U4 whose processor handles USB communication directly, with no separate USB-to-serial chip. This lets the board present itself to a computer as a native keyboard or mouse, so a sketch can type text or move the pointer, which is impossible on a standard Uno.

title: Arduino Micro
text: The Micro combines the Leonardo's ATmega32U4 and its native USB capability with a compact breadboard-friendly form factor. It is a good fit for custom input devices such as game controllers, macro keypads, and assistive switches that must be recognised by a computer without any driver installation.

title: Arduino Pro Mini
text: The Pro Mini strips out the USB connector to save space, cost, and power. Uploading requires an external USB-to-serial adapter connected to its programming header. It is intended for battery-powered and permanently installed projects where the USB port would never be used after the initial programming.

title: Arduino Due
text: The Due moves from 8-bit AVR to a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M3 running at 84 MHz, with far more memory and speed. Critically, its pins operate at 3.3V rather than 5V, so applying 5V to them can destroy the chip. Shields designed for 5V boards are not automatically compatible.

title: Arduino MKR family
text: The MKR boards share a compact 3.3V form factor aimed at connected projects. Different members add WiFi, LoRa, GSM, NB-IoT, or Ethernet while keeping a consistent pinout and a built-in lithium battery charging circuit. They suit remote sensing installations that must run on battery and report over a network.

title: Arduino Nano 33 IoT
text: The Nano 33 IoT keeps the small Nano footprint while adding a 32-bit processor, WiFi, Bluetooth, and a six-axis motion sensor. It runs at 3.3V. It is a practical choice for compact connected devices that need wireless communication without the size of a full MKR or Uno board.

title: Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense
text: The Nano 33 BLE Sense carries an unusually rich set of onboard sensors, including motion, magnetic field, pressure, humidity, temperature, light, gesture, and a microphone. Combined with Bluetooth Low Energy and support for on-device machine learning, it is often used for wearables and embedded audio or gesture recognition experiments.

title: Arduino Uno R4
text: The Uno R4 keeps the familiar Uno shape and 5V pin logic while replacing the 8-bit chip with a faster 32-bit Renesas processor offering much more memory. Two variants exist: a Minima, and a WiFi version that adds wireless connectivity and a small onboard LED matrix.

title: Clones and compatible boards
text: Because the designs are open, many manufacturers sell inexpensive compatible boards. They generally work identically, though some substitute a different USB-to-serial chip such as the CH340, which may require installing an extra driver. Build quality of voltage regulators and connectors varies more than on official boards.

title: Choosing a board for a project
text: Board selection usually comes down to four questions: how many pins the project needs, whether it must fit in a small enclosure, whether it needs wireless connectivity, and whether the attached components run at 5V or 3.3V. Starting with an Uno and migrating later is a common and low-risk approach.

title: Board pin logic voltage
text: Older AVR boards such as the Uno, Nano, and Mega use 5V logic. Newer boards including the Due, MKR family, and Nano 33 series use 3.3V. Connecting a 5V output to a 3.3V input can permanently damage the chip, so checking the logic voltage of both sides is essential.

title: The ATmega328P chip
text: The ATmega328P is the 8-bit AVR microcontroller at the heart of the Uno and classic Nano. It provides 32 KB of flash for program storage, 2 KB of SRAM for variables, and 1 KB of EEPROM for values that must survive a power cycle. It runs at 16 MHz.

title: Clock speed and instruction timing
text: A classic Arduino runs at 16 MHz, executing roughly sixteen million simple instructions per second. This is slow by desktop standards but ample for reading sensors and driving motors. It does impose limits on tasks such as high-rate audio sampling or driving large displays at speed.

title: Flash memory
text: Flash memory stores the compiled sketch and retains it without power. On an ATmega328P, 32 KB of flash is available, of which roughly half a kilobyte is occupied by the bootloader. When a sketch exceeds the remaining space the IDE refuses to upload and reports that the program is too large.

title: SRAM and running out of memory
text: SRAM holds variables while the program runs and is erased at power-off. The ATmega328P has only 2 KB, which is easily exhausted by large arrays or many text strings. Running out of SRAM rarely produces a clear error; instead the board behaves erratically, resets unexpectedly, or prints corrupted output.

title: EEPROM for persistent values
text: EEPROM is a small non-volatile memory intended for settings that must survive power loss, such as calibration values or a device identifier. It is accessed through the EEPROM library. Each cell tolerates only around one hundred thousand write cycles, so writing continuously inside the main loop will wear it out.

title: Saving SRAM with the F macro
text: By default every text string in a sketch is copied into scarce SRAM at startup. Wrapping a literal as F("text") keeps it in flash and reads it only when needed. On sketches with many printed messages this single change can free hundreds of bytes and cure mysterious instability.

title: The bootloader
text: The bootloader is a small program pre-installed in flash that runs briefly at every reset. It listens for an incoming sketch over the serial connection and writes it into flash, which is what allows uploading over plain USB with no hardware programmer. If no upload arrives it hands control to the stored sketch.

title: Programming without a bootloader
text: A sketch can be written directly through the ICSP header using a dedicated programmer or a second Arduino acting as one. This reclaims the bootloader's flash space and removes the reset delay, at the cost of needing extra hardware. It is also how a blank chip receives its bootloader initially.

title: Direct port manipulation
text: Behind digitalWrite lies a hardware register controlling eight pins at once. Writing those registers directly is dramatically faster and can change several pins simultaneously, which matters for timing-critical signalling. The cost is code that is harder to read and tied to one specific chip family.

title: 8-bit architecture implications
text: An 8-bit processor handles single bytes most efficiently. Arithmetic on larger types such as long or float requires multiple operations and is markedly slower. Choosing the smallest adequate data type, and avoiding floating point in tight loops, noticeably improves performance on classic AVR boards.

title: AVR compared with ARM boards
text: Classic boards use 8-bit AVR chips at 16 MHz with kilobytes of memory. Newer boards use 32-bit ARM cores running many times faster with far more memory and richer peripherals. Most sketches port across with little change, but code that manipulates registers directly is specific to one architecture.

title: Reading remaining memory
text: After compiling, the IDE reports how much flash the sketch occupies and estimates SRAM used by global variables. The SRAM figure excludes memory allocated while running, so a sketch reported as comfortable can still exhaust memory in practice. Leaving generous headroom is wise on 2 KB boards.

title: The pinMode function
text: Every digital pin must be told its direction before use. Calling pinMode with OUTPUT lets the pin drive a voltage, while INPUT configures it to sense one. This is normally done once inside setup. Forgetting it is a frequent cause of a circuit that appears wired correctly but does nothing.

title: The digitalWrite function
text: digitalWrite sets an output pin to HIGH, connecting it to the supply voltage, or LOW, connecting it to ground. This is how sketches switch LEDs, trigger relays, and send control signals. It has no effect on a pin still configured as an input, which is a common source of confusion.

title: The digitalRead function
text: digitalRead samples a digital pin and returns HIGH or LOW depending on whether the voltage is nearer the supply or ground. It is used to detect buttons, switches, and digital sensor outputs. The reading reflects the voltage at the instant of the call, so it is normally polled repeatedly.

title: Logic levels HIGH and LOW
text: On a 5V board, a pin above roughly three volts reads as HIGH and below about one and a half volts reads as LOW. Voltages between those thresholds are ambiguous and may read either way. Keeping signals firmly at supply or ground avoids unpredictable behaviour.

title: The INPUT_PULLUP mode
text: Configuring a pin as INPUT_PULLUP switches on a resistor inside the chip that gently holds the pin at the supply voltage. A button then connects the pin to ground when pressed. This removes the need for an external resistor, at the cost of inverted logic: the pin reads LOW when pressed.

title: Pull-up and pull-down resistors
text: A pull-up resistor ties an input to the supply voltage so it rests HIGH; a pull-down ties it to ground so it rests LOW. Either gives the pin a definite state when no switch is closed. Without one, the pin is left electrically undefined and its readings become unreliable.

title: Floating inputs
text: An input pin connected to nothing is described as floating. It behaves like a small antenna, picking up electrical noise and returning readings that change apparently at random, sometimes responding to a hand moving nearby. Every input must be anchored by a pull-up or pull-down resistor.

title: Current limits on a single pin
text: An output pin can supply roughly twenty milliamps comfortably, with an absolute ceiling near forty. This is enough for an indicator LED but nowhere near enough for a motor, a relay coil, or a strip of LEDs. Exceeding the limit damages the pin, often permanently and sometimes silently.

title: Total current across all pins
text: Beyond the per-pin limit, the whole chip has a combined ceiling of around two hundred milliamps through its supply and ground connections. Lighting many LEDs at once can breach this total even when each individual pin stays within its own limit, causing resets or gradual damage.

title: Wiring an LED safely
text: An LED must always be paired with a series resistor, typically between two hundred and one thousand ohms on a 5V board. The resistor limits current to a safe level. Connecting an LED directly between a pin and ground draws excessive current and will eventually destroy both the LED and the pin.

title: Wiring a push button
text: The simplest button circuit connects one side of the switch to a digital pin configured as INPUT_PULLUP and the other side to ground. No external components are needed. Pressing the button pulls the pin to ground, so the sketch tests for LOW rather than HIGH to detect a press.

title: Switch bounce and debouncing
text: Mechanical contacts do not close cleanly; they chatter for a few milliseconds, which the microcontroller reads as many rapid presses. Debouncing fixes this by ignoring further changes for a short interval after the first, or by requiring the reading to remain stable before accepting it as genuine.

title: The built-in LED on pin 13
text: Most boards include a small LED wired to digital pin thirteen through its own resistor. It requires no external components and is invaluable for confirming that a sketch is running or for signalling that a particular branch of code has been reached. The constant LED_BUILTIN refers to it portably.

title: Pins 0 and 1 conflict with USB
text: Digital pins zero and one are shared with the hardware serial port used for uploading and for the serial monitor. Connecting components to them can block uploads or corrupt serial output. Unless the project genuinely needs a second serial device, it is best to leave both pins free.

title: Level shifting between voltages
text: Connecting a 5V board to a 3.3V sensor requires reducing the signal voltage, using a level shifter module or a simple resistor divider on the line feeding the sensor. Skipping this step may work briefly but stresses the 3.3V device and often leads to gradual, hard-to-diagnose failure.

title: The analogRead function
text: analogRead measures the voltage on an analog input pin and returns a number representing it. This allows continuously variable quantities such as temperature, light level, or knob position to be brought into a sketch, unlike digital pins which report only two states.

title: Ten-bit analog resolution
text: The analog-to-digital converter on classic Arduino boards has ten-bit resolution, producing values from zero to one thousand and twenty-three. Zero corresponds to ground and the maximum to the reference voltage, so on a 5V board each step represents just under five millivolts.

title: Analog reference voltage
text: Readings are measured against a reference voltage, by default the board's supply. Because that supply can sag under load, readings may drift as motors or LEDs switch on. Selecting the internal reference or supplying a stable external one gives far more repeatable measurements.

title: The analogReference function
text: analogReference selects which voltage the converter compares against. The internal option on an ATmega328P is around 1.1 volts, which greatly improves resolution when measuring small signals. After changing the reference, the first reading or two should be discarded while the input settles.

title: Analog input pins
text: The Uno provides six analog inputs labelled A0 through A5, while the Mega offers sixteen. They connect to a single converter through an internal multiplexer, meaning only one channel is sampled at any moment. Reading several in quick succession is fine, but they are not sampled simultaneously.

title: Analog pins used as digital pins
text: Analog input pins can also serve as ordinary digital pins, referenced by name as A0 and so on. This is a useful way to recover extra digital capacity on a crowded Uno. The reverse is not true: a plain digital pin cannot perform analog measurement.

title: Voltage dividers
text: A voltage divider uses two resistors in series to produce a proportionally smaller voltage from a larger one. It allows an Arduino to measure a battery voltage above its own supply, and forms the basis of circuits reading resistive sensors such as light-dependent resistors and thermistors.

title: Reading a potentiometer
text: A potentiometer wired with its outer legs to supply and ground and its middle leg to an analog pin acts as an adjustable voltage divider. Turning the shaft sweeps the reading across its full range, making it the simplest way to add a manual control to a project.

title: The map function
text: map rescales a number from one range into another, for example converting a sensor reading spanning zero to one thousand and twenty-three into a brightness value spanning zero to two hundred and fifty-five. It uses integer arithmetic, so fractional parts are discarded rather than rounded.

title: Noise in analog readings
text: Analog readings commonly fluctuate by a few counts even with a steady input, caused by electrical noise and supply variation. Averaging several consecutive samples, adding a small capacitor near the sensor, and keeping signal wires short and away from motor wiring all reduce the effect.

title: Analog reading speed
text: Each analogRead takes roughly one hundred microseconds, which caps sampling at about ten thousand readings per second. This is generous for temperature or light sensing but restrictive for audio work. Tight loops calling analogRead many times can therefore run much slower than expected.

title: No true analog output on classic boards
text: Classic Arduino boards cannot produce a genuine variable voltage; they only switch pins fully on or off. What is called analog output is really a rapidly pulsed digital signal. Boards such as the Due include a real digital-to-analog converter that can output an actual intermediate voltage.

title: Pulse width modulation explained
text: Pulse width modulation switches a pin on and off very rapidly and varies the proportion of time it spends on. Devices that respond slowly, such as an LED viewed by the eye or a motor with rotational inertia, react to the average, producing an apparently intermediate brightness or speed.

title: The analogWrite function
text: analogWrite sets the pulse width on a PWM-capable pin, accepting a value from zero for permanently off to two hundred and fifty-five for permanently on. Despite the name it does not produce a true analog voltage. The pin does not need pinMode called first, though setting it as OUTPUT is clearer.

title: Which pins support PWM
text: Only certain pins can produce PWM, marked on the board with a tilde symbol beside the number. On the Uno these are pins three, five, six, nine, ten, and eleven. Calling analogWrite on any other pin simply switches it fully on or off with no intermediate levels.

title: PWM frequency
text: The default switching frequency is roughly 490 hertz on most pins and about 980 hertz on two of them. This is fast enough to be invisible in an LED but slow enough to produce an audible whine in some motors. The frequency can be raised by reconfiguring the underlying timer.

title: Dimming an LED
text: Fading an LED is the classic demonstration of PWM: a loop steps the analogWrite value gradually from zero up to two hundred and fifty-five and back. Because human brightness perception is non-linear, a linear sweep looks uneven, with most of the visible change happening at the low end.

title: Controlling motor speed with PWM
text: PWM sets the speed of a DC motor by varying the average voltage reaching it. The signal must drive a transistor or motor driver rather than the motor itself, since motors draw far more current than a pin can supply. At very low duty cycles a motor may buzz without turning.

title: PWM value range
text: analogWrite accepts values from zero to two hundred and fifty-five, giving 256 discrete levels regardless of the analog input range of zero to one thousand and twenty-three. Passing a sensor reading straight through without rescaling is a frequent mistake, since values above 255 simply saturate.

title: Smoothing PWM into a real voltage
text: Placing a resistor and capacitor low-pass filter on a PWM output averages the pulses into a genuine steady voltage. This provides a crude digital-to-analog converter for driving analog meters or control inputs. Higher PWM frequencies allow smaller filter components and less residual ripple.

title: Starting serial communication
text: Serial.begin opens the serial port and must be called in setup before any serial output. Its argument sets the communication speed in bits per second, most commonly 9600 or 115200. Without this call, printed output never appears and the serial monitor stays blank.

title: Baud rate matching
text: The speed set in the sketch must match the speed selected in the serial monitor. A mismatch does not produce silence but a stream of meaningless symbols, which is one of the most commonly reported beginner problems and is fixed by aligning both settings.

title: The serial monitor
text: The serial monitor is a window in the IDE displaying text sent from the board and allowing text to be typed back. It is the primary debugging tool on a platform with no screen or debugger, letting a sketch report variable values and progress as it runs.

title: Printing values
text: Serial.print sends text or a number without a line break, while Serial.println adds one. Numbers can be printed in decimal, hexadecimal, or binary by passing a second argument, and floats accept a digit count. Combining several prints builds up a readable labelled line of diagnostic output.

title: Reading incoming serial data
text: Serial.available reports how many bytes have arrived and are waiting, and Serial.read removes the next one. Checking available before reading avoids consuming data that has not yet arrived. This pair underpins simple command interfaces where typed input controls the running sketch.

title: The serial plotter
text: The serial plotter graphs numbers sent over serial as live scrolling traces. Printing several values separated by spaces or commas draws multiple lines together. It makes trends, noise, and oscillation in sensor data immediately visible in a way that scrolling text does not.

title: Hardware serial pins
text: The hardware serial port on an Uno is wired to digital pins zero and one, which are also connected to the USB interface. Anything attached to those pins competes with the USB connection, so they should generally be left unused when the serial monitor is needed.

title: The USB-to-serial converter
text: The microcontroller speaks serial, not USB, so boards include a separate chip translating between them. Official Unos use an ATmega16U2 while many clones use a CH340 needing an extra driver. If no port appears in the IDE, a missing driver for this chip is a likely cause.

title: The SoftwareSerial library
text: SoftwareSerial creates additional serial ports on ordinary digital pins by generating the timing in software. This frees the hardware port for the serial monitor while a module such as a Bluetooth adapter uses other pins. It is slower, consumes processor time, and struggles above about 38400 baud.

title: Serial devices blocking uploads
text: A device connected to pins zero and one can interfere with the upload process, producing a synchronisation error. Temporarily disconnecting those wires, uploading, then reconnecting them is the standard remedy, and is a strong argument for placing peripherals on other pins from the start.

title: Debugging by printing
text: With no step debugger available, inserting print statements is the usual way to understand a misbehaving sketch. Printing at the start of functions confirms which code runs, and printing variable values reveals where a calculation goes wrong. Removing them afterwards recovers both speed and program space.

title: The serial buffer
text: Incoming serial data is held in a buffer of only sixty-four bytes. If a sketch is slow to read it, further bytes are discarded without warning, producing truncated messages. Reading promptly inside the loop, or sending data in smaller pieces, avoids the loss.

title: What I2C is
text: I2C is a communication bus that connects many devices using just two shared wires plus ground. Each device has its own address, so sensors, displays, and memory chips can coexist on the same pair of wires. It greatly reduces pin usage compared with wiring each device separately.

title: The Wire library
text: The Wire library provides I2C support and is bundled with the IDE. Wire.begin starts the bus, and transmissions are framed by beginTransmission and endTransmission with data queued in between. Most sensor libraries build on Wire, so it is often used indirectly rather than called explicitly.

title: I2C pins on common boards
text: On the Uno the I2C signals appear on analog pins four and five, labelled SDA and SCL. On the Mega they are pins twenty and twenty-one. Many boards also duplicate them on dedicated headers near the USB connector, which is convenient for stacking shields.

title: Device addresses
text: Every device on an I2C bus needs a unique seven-bit address. Two identical sensors therefore conflict unless one can be readdressed, usually by soldering a jumper or tying an address pin to a different level. Address clashes typically appear as one device working and the other being invisible.

title: Scanning the I2C bus
text: An I2C scanner sketch attempts communication with every possible address and prints those that respond. It is the fastest way to confirm that wiring is correct and to discover the actual address of a module, which frequently differs from the value printed in its datasheet or tutorial.

title: Pull-up resistors on I2C
text: Both I2C lines require pull-up resistors to function. Most breakout boards include them, so a single module usually works with no extra parts. Stacking several modules places their resistors in parallel, which can over-load the bus and require removing the pull-ups from all but one board.

title: I2C bus length and speed
text: I2C is designed for short connections within a single device, typically well under a metre. Standard speed is one hundred kilohertz with a faster four hundred kilohertz mode widely supported. Long wires add capacitance that rounds the signal edges and produces intermittent, confusing communication failures.

title: Common I2C peripherals
text: Widely used I2C devices include the SSD1306 OLED display, the BMP280 pressure sensor, the MPU6050 motion sensor, the DS3231 real-time clock, and character LCD backpack adapters. Their popularity means well-tested libraries and abundant wiring examples are readily available.

title: What SPI is
text: SPI is a fast synchronous communication bus using separate wires for outgoing data, incoming data, and a clock, plus one select line per device. It is considerably quicker than I2C, which makes it the usual choice for displays, SD cards, and radio modules that move larger volumes of data.

title: SPI signal lines
text: SPI uses MOSI carrying data from the Arduino to the device, MISO carrying data back, and SCK providing the clock. A further select line activates one device at a time. On an Uno these occupy digital pins eleven, twelve, and thirteen respectively.

title: The SPI library
text: The bundled SPI library handles the low-level signalling. A sketch begins a transaction specifying clock speed and mode, transfers bytes, then ends the transaction. Transactions matter when several devices share the bus at different speeds, as they restore the correct settings for each one.

title: Choosing between SPI and I2C
text: SPI offers much higher throughput but consumes an extra pin for every additional device. I2C needs only two wires no matter how many devices are attached but runs slower. Bulk transfers such as refreshing a graphical display favour SPI, while collections of small sensors favour I2C.

title: The ICSP header
text: The six-pin ICSP header exposes the SPI signals along with reset and power. It provides a route for hardware programmers to write firmware directly, and lets shields reach the SPI pins in a way that works across boards whose pin numbering differs, such as the Uno and the Mega.

title: Multiple devices on one SPI bus
text: Several SPI devices share the data and clock lines but each requires its own select pin held low only while that device is being addressed. Forgetting to raise the others is a common fault, causing two devices to respond at once and corrupting the data.

title: The setup function
text: setup runs once when the board powers up or resets. It is where pin directions are declared, serial communication is opened, and libraries are initialised. Code that needs to happen only once at the beginning belongs here rather than in the repeating main loop.

title: The loop function
text: loop runs repeatedly for as long as the board has power, restarting the moment it finishes. This continuous repetition is the core of Arduino's execution model. Everything that must happen continuously, such as reading sensors and updating outputs, is driven from inside it.

title: Variables and data types
text: A variable reserves memory and is declared with a type fixing what it holds and how much space it uses. Choosing an appropriately small type matters on boards with only two kilobytes of SRAM, where careless use of large types in arrays quickly exhausts available memory.

title: Integer types
text: An int on a classic AVR board holds sixteen bits, spanning roughly minus thirty-two thousand to plus thirty-two thousand. A byte holds zero to two hundred and fifty-five, and a long holds thirty-two bits. On 32-bit boards an int is thirty-two bits, so code relying on overflow may behave differently.

title: Floating point numbers
text: The float type stores fractional values with about six or seven significant digits of precision. AVR chips have no floating-point hardware, so such arithmetic is emulated in software and runs far slower than integer maths. Working in whole units such as millivolts often avoids floats entirely.

title: Boolean values
text: A boolean variable holds only true or false and is the natural choice for flags such as whether a light is currently on or a threshold has been crossed. Using booleans instead of integers makes intent obvious to a reader and keeps conditional logic straightforward.

title: Arrays
text: An array stores a numbered sequence of values of one type under a single name, ideal for a set of pins or a history of readings. Indices start at zero, so the last element of a ten-item array is index nine. Reading past the end corrupts memory without any error message.

title: Conditional statements
text: An if statement runs a block only when a condition is true, with optional else if and else branches for alternatives. Conditions combine comparisons using logical and and or. A frequent error is writing a single equals sign, which assigns a value rather than comparing two.

title: For loops
text: A for loop repeats a block a known number of times using a counter that it initialises, tests, and advances. It suits stepping through an array of pins or fading a value across a range, replacing long stretches of near-identical repeated statements.

title: While loops
text: A while loop repeats for as long as its condition remains true, suiting situations where the number of repetitions is unknown, such as waiting for input. Because it blocks everything else until it exits, a while loop in the main path can make a sketch appear frozen.

title: Writing functions
text: A function groups statements under a name so they can be called from several places. It declares a return type and may accept parameters. Splitting a long loop into well-named functions such as readSensors and updateDisplay makes a sketch substantially easier to follow and to modify.

title: Constants
text: Marking a value const tells the compiler it never changes, which catches accidental modification and can save memory. Naming pins and thresholds as constants at the top of a sketch means rewiring requires editing one line rather than hunting for scattered numbers throughout the code.

title: Comments
text: Text after two slashes is ignored to the end of the line, and text between slash-star and star-slash is ignored across multiple lines. Good comments explain why a choice was made rather than restating what the code plainly does, which is the part a later reader cannot reconstruct.

title: Strings versus character arrays
text: The String class is convenient and supports easy concatenation, but repeated manipulation fragments the small heap and can destabilise long-running sketches. Fixed character arrays are less comfortable to use but entirely predictable, which is why they are preferred for code expected to run for weeks.

title: Variable scope
text: A variable declared inside a function exists only while that function runs and is recreated on each call. One declared outside all functions is global, persists for the program's lifetime, and is visible everywhere. State that must survive between loop iterations therefore has to be global or static.

title: The switch statement
text: A switch selects among several branches based on one value, offering a clearer alternative to a long chain of else if tests. Each case normally ends with break; omitting it causes execution to fall through into the following case, which is occasionally intended but usually a bug.

title: Static variables
text: Declaring a local variable static makes it retain its value between calls while keeping it hidden from the rest of the program. It is a tidy way to hold state such as a last-seen reading inside the one function that uses it, avoiding an unnecessary global.

title: Integer division and overflow
text: Dividing two integers discards any remainder, so a calculation expected to yield a fraction silently returns a whole number. Similarly, arithmetic exceeding a type's range wraps around without warning. Both produce results that look plausible but are wrong, making them awkward to spot.

title: The delay function
text: delay pauses the sketch for a given number of milliseconds. It is the simplest way to control timing and appears in nearly every introductory example, such as blinking an LED once per second by alternating the pin state with pauses in between.

title: Why delay causes problems
text: During a delay the sketch does nothing else: it cannot read buttons, respond to sensors, or service communication. A project that must react promptly while also timing events will feel unresponsive, missing button presses that happen to occur during the pause.

title: The millis function
text: millis returns the number of milliseconds since the board started running. Rather than pausing, a sketch records the time an event occurred and later checks whether enough time has elapsed. This keeps the loop running freely and is the foundation of responsive Arduino code.

title: The non-blocking timing pattern
text: The standard pattern stores a previous timestamp, then each pass through the loop tests whether the current millis value minus that timestamp exceeds the desired interval. When it does, the action runs and the timestamp updates. Several such timers can run concurrently at different rates.

title: Millis rollover
text: The millisecond counter overflows back to zero after roughly forty-nine days. Comparing elapsed time by subtracting the stored timestamp from the current value handles this correctly through unsigned arithmetic, whereas comparing against a precomputed target time breaks at the moment of rollover.

title: The micros function
text: micros counts microseconds since startup, providing finer resolution for measuring short intervals such as an ultrasonic echo. Its resolution is four microseconds on classic boards and it overflows after about seventy minutes, so it suits brief measurements rather than long-term timekeeping.

title: The delayMicroseconds function
text: delayMicroseconds provides very short pauses for protocols requiring precise pulse widths, such as triggering an ultrasonic sensor or driving addressable LEDs. It is accurate for values up to a few thousand microseconds; longer waits should use delay or a millis-based timer instead.

title: State machines
text: A state machine tracks which stage a process has reached in a variable and acts accordingly on each pass through the loop. It expresses sequences such as waiting, running, and cooling down without blocking, and scales far better than nested delays as project behaviour grows more complex.

title: Hardware timers
text: AVR chips contain several hardware timers that count independently of the running program, underpinning millis, PWM, and the tone function. Reconfiguring one changes the behaviour of whatever else depends on it, so altering a timer to change PWM frequency can quietly break millis timing.

title: Keeping accurate long-term time
text: Arduino's internal timing drifts by seconds per day and resets whenever power is lost, making it unsuitable for a clock. A real-time clock module such as the DS3231 keeps accurate time with its own battery and reports the date and time over I2C when asked.

title: What interrupts do
text: An interrupt lets the processor abandon the main program the instant a signal changes, run a short handler, then resume where it left off. This catches brief events that a polling loop would miss, such as a fast pulse arriving while the sketch is busy elsewhere.

title: The attachInterrupt function
text: attachInterrupt binds a function to a pin and specifies which kind of change should trigger it. The pin number must be wrapped in digitalPinToInterrupt for portability across boards, since the mapping between pin numbers and interrupt channels differs between an Uno and a Mega.

title: Which pins support interrupts
text: On the Uno only digital pins two and three can trigger external interrupts. The Leonardo offers five such pins and the Mega six, while many newer 32-bit boards allow almost any pin. Wiring a time-critical signal to a non-interrupt pin is a common oversight.

title: Rules for interrupt handlers
text: A handler must finish quickly and do as little as possible. Inside one, delay does not work, millis stops advancing, and serial printing is unreliable. The usual approach is to set a flag or capture a value, then let the main loop perform the real work when it next runs.

title: The volatile keyword
text: Any variable shared between an interrupt handler and the main program must be declared volatile. Without it the compiler may cache the value in a register and never notice the handler changing it, producing a sketch that works at low optimisation and fails mysteriously otherwise.

title: Interrupt trigger modes
text: An interrupt can fire on RISING when a signal goes from low to high, on FALLING for the opposite, on CHANGE for either, or on LOW while the pin is held down. Choosing the wrong mode commonly causes a handler to run twice per event instead of once.

title: Reading multi-byte values safely
text: A value larger than one byte that an interrupt updates can be read half-updated by the main program, yielding a nonsensical result. Briefly disabling interrupts around the read, then re-enabling them, guarantees a consistent copy. The disabled window must be kept as short as possible.

title: Powering over USB
text: A USB connection supplies five volts and typically up to five hundred milliamps, which comfortably runs the board and modest sensors. It is the usual arrangement during development. Motors and LED strips generally exceed what a USB port will provide and need their own supply.

title: The barrel jack and VIN
text: The barrel jack accepts an unregulated supply which passes through the onboard regulator, as does the VIN pin. Seven to twelve volts is the recommended range. Higher voltages make the regulator run hot and waste the excess as heat, while lower ones leave the five volt rail unstable.

title: The onboard voltage regulator
text: A linear regulator converts the input voltage down to five volts, dissipating the difference as heat. Supplying twelve volts while drawing significant current makes it uncomfortably hot and may trigger thermal shutdown. Feeding a lower input voltage or using an external switching supply avoids the problem.

title: The 5V and 3.3V pins
text: The 5V pin outputs the regulated supply and can power external components within the regulator's limits. The 3.3V pin comes from a much smaller regulator, typically supplying only about fifty milliamps. Overloading the 3.3V pin causes resets and is easy to do with wireless modules.

title: Never back-feed the 5V pin
text: Applying an external five volt supply to the 5V pin bypasses the regulator and the protection circuitry. Doing so while USB is also connected can drive current back into the computer's port. If an external regulated supply is used, the USB cable should be disconnected.

title: Running from batteries
text: A nine volt battery connected to the barrel jack works but drains quickly because the regulator wastes much of the voltage. Four AA cells giving six volts, or a lithium cell with a suitable regulator, deliver considerably longer runtime for the same physical size.

title: Typical current consumption
text: An Uno running an ordinary sketch draws roughly forty to fifty milliamps, largely due to the regulator and onboard LEDs rather than the microcontroller itself. A bare ATmega328P without those extras draws only a few milliamps, which is why battery projects often omit the full board.

title: Sleep modes
text: The microcontroller can be put into a sleep state where most of it stops, cutting consumption to microamps. A timer or an interrupt on a pin wakes it. For a sensor that reports once an hour, sleeping between readings extends battery life from days to months.

title: Separate supplies for motors
text: Motors, servos, and relays draw far more current than the board can deliver and produce voltage dips that reset the microcontroller. They should be powered from their own supply. The classic symptom of ignoring this is a board that restarts every time a motor begins to turn.

title: Sharing a common ground
text: When a project uses more than one power supply, all grounds must be connected together. Without a shared ground reference, signals between the sections have no common baseline and communication fails or behaves erratically. This single missing wire causes a large share of multi-supply faults.

title: Decoupling capacitors
text: Small capacitors placed close to a chip's power pins supply brief current surges and smooth the local voltage. Without them, fast switching produces dips that cause unexplained resets and corrupted readings. A hundred nanofarad capacitor near each device is standard practice on any permanent build.

title: How sensors interface with Arduino
text: Sensors report in one of three ways: a varying voltage read with analogRead, a simple on or off state read with digitalRead, or a digital message exchanged over I2C or SPI. Identifying which category a sensor falls into is the first step in wiring and programming it.

title: Light-dependent resistors
text: A light-dependent resistor changes resistance with illumination, falling as light increases. Wired as one half of a voltage divider, it produces a voltage an analog pin can read. It is inexpensive and ideal for detecting whether a room is lit or triggering a night light.

title: The TMP36 temperature sensor
text: The TMP36 outputs a voltage proportional to temperature, requiring only a single analog pin and no library. Converting the reading involves subtracting a fixed offset and scaling. Its simplicity makes it a common first temperature sensor, though accuracy is modest at around two degrees.

title: DHT11 and DHT22 sensors
text: The DHT family measures temperature and humidity together and communicates over a single data wire using its own protocol, handled by a library. The DHT22 is more accurate and works over a wider range than the cheaper DHT11. Both respond slowly and should not be polled more than every two seconds.

title: The DS18B20 temperature sensor
text: The DS18B20 is a digital temperature sensor communicating over a one-wire bus, allowing many sensors to share a single data pin since each carries a unique serial number. Waterproof probe versions are common in aquarium, brewing, and heating monitoring projects.

title: The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor
text: The HC-SR04 measures distance by emitting an ultrasonic pulse and timing the echo. The sketch sends a brief trigger pulse then measures how long the echo pin stays high, converting that duration to distance using the speed of sound. It works reliably from a few centimetres to about four metres.

title: PIR motion sensors
text: A passive infrared sensor detects the movement of a warm body by sensing changes in infrared radiation. It outputs a simple high or low signal needing only digitalRead. Onboard trimmers usually adjust sensitivity and how long the output stays active after motion stops.

title: Tilt and vibration switches
text: A tilt switch contains a rolling ball that closes a contact at a particular orientation, while a vibration switch closes briefly when shaken. Both behave like simple buttons and are read with digitalRead, making them a cheap way to detect movement or a knock.

title: Reed switches
text: A reed switch closes when a magnet comes near and is read exactly like a button. Because the two halves need no electrical connection, it is the standard way to sense whether a door or window is closed, with the magnet mounted on the moving part.

title: The MPU6050 motion sensor
text: The MPU6050 combines a three-axis accelerometer and a three-axis gyroscope on one I2C module. It reports acceleration and rotation rate, from which tilt and movement are derived. Self-balancing robots, gesture controllers, and motion-activated devices commonly rely on it.

title: Barometric pressure sensors
text: The BMP280 and BME280 measure atmospheric pressure and temperature over I2C, with the BME280 adding humidity. Because pressure falls predictably with altitude, they also serve as altimeters, and are widely used in weather stations and model rocket or drone projects.

title: Soil moisture sensors
text: A soil moisture sensor infers water content from the electrical properties of soil between two probes and reports an analog value. Cheap resistive versions corrode quickly because current flows through the soil; capacitive versions avoid this and last far longer in permanent plant-watering installations.

title: MQ series gas sensors
text: MQ sensors detect gases such as smoke, carbon monoxide, methane, or alcohol vapour, returning an analog reading that rises with concentration. They contain a heater needing several minutes to stabilise, and give relative rather than calibrated readings unless carefully characterised against a known source.

title: Hall effect sensors
text: A Hall effect sensor responds to magnetic fields, with digital versions switching when a magnet is near and analog versions reporting field strength. Attaching a magnet to a rotating shaft and counting pulses is a standard technique for measuring wheel or fan speed.

title: Rotary encoders
text: A rotary encoder reports rotation as a sequence of pulses on two pins, and the order in which they change reveals the direction. Unlike a potentiometer it turns endlessly with no stops, making it well suited to menu navigation and adjusting values on a display.

title: Force and flex sensors
text: A force sensitive resistor lowers its resistance as pressure increases, while a flex sensor changes resistance as it bends. Both are read through a voltage divider on an analog pin. They appear in touch-sensitive interfaces, robotic grippers, and instrumented glove projects.

title: Colour and gesture sensors
text: Colour sensors such as the TCS34725 report red, green, and blue intensity over I2C, allowing an Arduino to identify the colour of a nearby object. Related modules add proximity and simple gesture recognition, detecting a hand swiping left, right, up, or down.

title: Current sensing
text: Current sensors such as the ACS712 output a voltage proportional to the current flowing through them, letting a sketch monitor power consumption or detect a stalled motor. They must be wired in series with the load, unlike voltage measurements which connect in parallel.

title: Sensor calibration
text: Few inexpensive sensors are accurate straight from the packet. Calibration compares readings against a known reference and derives a correction, whether a simple offset or a scaling factor. Storing those constants in EEPROM lets a device keep its calibration across power cycles.

title: What actuators do
text: Actuators convert electrical signals into physical effects: light, sound, movement, or heat. Because nearly all of them draw more current than a pin can supply, the recurring design question is not how to command them but how to switch the power they need safely.

title: Driving LEDs
text: A single indicator LED connects through a current-limiting resistor to a digital pin. Several LEDs may exceed the chip's total current limit, in which case a transistor or dedicated driver chip carries the load while the pin merely controls it.

title: RGB LEDs
text: An RGB LED contains red, green, and blue emitters in one package with a shared pin. Driving each colour from a PWM pin mixes arbitrary colours. Common anode types share a positive connection and are dimmed by lowering the pin, which inverts the expected values.

title: Piezo buzzers and the tone function
text: A piezo buzzer produces sound when driven with an alternating signal. The tone function generates a square wave at a chosen frequency on a pin, allowing beeps, alarms, and simple melodies. It uses a hardware timer, which can conflict with PWM on certain pins.

title: Hobby servo motors
text: A hobby servo moves to a commanded angle, typically anywhere within about one hundred and eighty degrees, and holds that position. It has three wires for power, ground, and control, and contains its own feedback electronics, so no external driver circuit is required.

title: The Servo library
text: The Servo library generates the pulse train servos expect, so a sketch simply writes an angle in degrees. It supports up to twelve servos on an Uno but disables PWM on pins nine and ten while in use, which surprises sketches that also dim an LED there.

title: Powering servos
text: A servo under load can draw several hundred milliamps and produces sharp current spikes as it moves. Powering one from the board's 5V pin frequently causes resets. A separate supply, with grounds joined to the Arduino, is the reliable arrangement for anything beyond a single small servo.

title: DC motors
text: A brushed DC motor spins continuously when supplied with voltage, its speed varying with the average voltage applied. It cannot be connected to a pin directly under any circumstances, since even a small motor draws far more current than the chip can survive.

title: H-bridge motor drivers
text: An H-bridge lets a motor be driven in both directions by reversing the polarity across it electronically. Modules based on the L298N or newer, more efficient chips accept direction and PWM speed inputs from the Arduino while handling the motor current on a separate supply.

title: Transistors as switches
text: A transistor lets a small pin current control a much larger one. A MOSFET or bipolar transistor between the load and ground switches motors, lamps, and heaters on command. This is the standard low-cost solution whenever a device draws more than a pin can safely deliver.

title: Flyback diodes
text: Switching off a motor, relay, or solenoid causes its coil to generate a large reverse voltage spike capable of destroying the driving transistor. A diode placed across the coil gives that energy a safe path to dissipate. Omitting it leads to failures that appear only after many switching cycles.

title: Stepper motors
text: A stepper motor rotates in fixed increments rather than spinning freely, so its position is known without any feedback sensor. This makes it the standard choice for 3D printers, camera sliders, and small CNC machines where repeatable positioning matters more than speed.

title: Driving stepper motors
text: Steppers need a driver that energises their coils in the correct sequence, such as a ULN2003 board for small motors or an A4988 for larger ones. The Stepper and AccelStepper libraries handle the sequencing, with AccelStepper adding smooth acceleration and simultaneous control of several motors.

title: Relay modules
text: A relay is an electrically operated mechanical switch, letting a low-voltage signal control a completely separate circuit. Relay modules include the driver transistor and protection diode already fitted. They are the usual way to switch mains-powered appliances, which demands proper insulation and considerable care.

title: Solenoids and locks
text: A solenoid converts current into a short linear push or pull and is commonly found in electric door locks and pneumatic valves. Like a relay coil it is inductive, so it needs a transistor driver, a flyback diode, and its own supply rather than the board's regulator.

title: Character LCD displays
text: The 16x2 character LCD shows two rows of sixteen characters and is a long-standing choice for showing readings and menus. It needs no graphics handling, just text positioned by row and column, which keeps both the wiring and the code straightforward.

title: The LiquidCrystal library
text: The bundled LiquidCrystal library drives character LCDs in parallel mode, using six digital pins. The sketch declares which pins are connected, sets the display dimensions, positions the cursor, and prints text much as it would to the serial monitor.

title: I2C LCD backpacks
text: A small adapter board soldered to a character LCD converts it to I2C, cutting the connection from six pins to two. Given how quickly an Uno runs short of pins, this is almost always the better option, needing only a different library and the module's I2C address.

title: OLED displays
text: SSD1306 OLED modules provide a small graphical display over I2C, typically 128 by 64 pixels. They render crisp text, simple shapes, and bitmaps with excellent contrast and no backlight. Their main constraint is the buffer they consume in the Arduino's limited SRAM.

title: Seven-segment displays
text: Seven-segment displays show digits using individually lit bars and suit clocks and counters where only numbers are needed. Multi-digit modules driven by a chip such as the MAX7219 reduce the wiring to a few pins and handle the rapid multiplexing themselves.

title: LED matrix displays
text: An LED matrix arranges LEDs in a grid to display characters, simple graphics, or scrolling messages. Modules based on the MAX7219 chain together over a few shared pins, so several panels can form a long scrolling sign controlled from a single Arduino.

title: Addressable LED strips
text: WS2812 strips, often sold as NeoPixels, give each LED its own controller so an entire strip is driven from one data pin with individual colour control. They draw substantial current at full brightness, commonly requiring a dedicated supply rather than the Arduino's regulator.

title: Colour TFT displays
text: Small TFT screens communicating over SPI provide full colour graphics for gauges, menus, and images. They demand more processing and memory than character or OLED displays, so classic 8-bit boards refresh them slowly and newer 32-bit boards give noticeably better results.

title: Bluetooth with HC-05 modules
text: The HC-05 provides a wireless serial link that a phone or computer sees as an ordinary serial port. Since the sketch simply reads and writes serial data, adding basic remote control needs almost no code change from a wired version, which explains its enduring popularity.

title: Bluetooth Low Energy
text: Bluetooth Low Energy suits battery devices sending small amounts of data infrequently. Rather than emulating a serial port it exposes named characteristics that a phone app reads and writes. Boards such as the Nano 33 BLE include it directly with library support.

title: ESP8266 WiFi modules
text: The ESP8266 adds WiFi and is often attached to an Arduino as a serial peripheral driven by text commands. It runs at 3.3V and draws current spikes during transmission, so a 5V board needs level shifting and a supply capable of handling the surges.

title: Boards with integrated WiFi
text: Boards including the MKR WiFi, Nano 33 IoT, and Uno R4 WiFi build wireless connectivity into the board itself. This removes the level shifting, extra wiring, and power problems of bolt-on modules, and is usually the simpler route for a new connected project.

title: nRF24L01 radio modules
text: The nRF24L01 provides low-cost two-way radio between Arduinos over tens of metres without any WiFi network. It communicates over SPI at 3.3V. Many reliability complaints trace back to inadequate power, cured by a capacitor across the module's supply pins.

title: LoRa for long range
text: LoRa trades data rate for range, carrying small messages several kilometres in open country at very low power. It suits remote sensors in fields, farms, or hillsides where no WiFi exists, reporting occasional readings on batteries lasting months.

title: Ethernet shields
text: An Ethernet shield gives a wired network connection, which is more reliable than wireless in electrically noisy places such as workshops. The board can then serve a small web page for control or push readings to a server, without the complications of wireless configuration.

title: MQTT and IoT platforms
text: MQTT is a lightweight publish and subscribe protocol widely used for connected devices. An Arduino publishes readings to a topic on a broker, and dashboards or home automation systems subscribe to it. This decouples the device from its consumers and suits intermittent, low-bandwidth links.

title: What libraries provide
text: A library packages the code needed to work with a component so a sketch calls simple named functions instead of implementing a protocol. Nearly every sensor, display, and radio module has one, which is why unfamiliar hardware can often be working within minutes.

title: Installing libraries
text: The Library Manager inside the IDE searches a curated index and installs with one click, handling updates too. Libraries distributed as a zip file elsewhere can be added through the import option. Manual copying into the libraries folder works but is easy to get wrong.

title: Boards manager and third-party boards
text: The Boards Manager installs support for board families beyond the built-in set. Adding a URL for a third-party package makes boards such as ESP8266 and ESP32 targets appear in the board menu, letting them be programmed from the familiar Arduino environment.

title: Example sketches
text: Every installed library brings example sketches reachable from the File menu. Opening a working example and confirming the hardware responds before writing original code isolates wiring faults from programming faults, and is the fastest way to bring up an unfamiliar component.

title: Home automation projects
text: Home automation is a common Arduino application: switching lights and appliances through relays, reading temperature to control heating, or detecting whether a door is open. Adding a network connection lets these be monitored and controlled remotely or integrated into an existing smart home system.

title: Robotics and data logging
text: Robots pair motor drivers with distance and line sensors so an Arduino can navigate autonomously. Data logging projects instead record sensor readings to an SD card or a network service with timestamps from a real-time clock, producing datasets for weather, energy use, or environmental monitoring.
